selected_news.title: Karamoja’da kuraklık: Tek öğünle yaşam ve su damlaları
selected_news.summary: African countries at the UN climate summit in Turkey are demanding more funding from developed nations to help them cope with climate change.
selected_news.source_headline: More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
selected_news.article_text: In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable "Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC "Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up." Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village "As we reached a safe height, we saw our house swept away right in front of our eyes. Everything I had was gone," he told the BBC He lost a harvest of 15 bags of sorghum and part of his farmland. His children were so traumatised that they stopped going to school "They refused to go to school for many months. They were so disturbed," he recalled After relocating and trying to rebuild his life, Nkhambala is now facing another climate challenge - this time a lack of rain "This time we fear there may be no harvest. I have no clue what I will do." A government assessment after Cyclone Freddy found that Malawi had experienced more than 50 disasters linked to storms, floods, landslides and droughts since 1980, affecting millions of people While Uganda and Malawi are suffering the effects of climate change and their governments are asking for assistance adapting to the new global weather patterns, they are among 23 African countries yet to submit National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) to the UN climate convention secretariat These are the plans that detail how climate change has affected them and the risks they face, and so help make a case for what assistance they need. Without them, experts say, it becomes difficult to secure funding "Our region has experienced cyclical droughts for decades, but there has been no action plan to tackle these climate impacts," said Milton Lorpia, who works for Warrior Squad Foundation in Karamoja region of Uganda "If only such a plan were in place and implemented, it would certainly have helped us." The African Group of Negotiators at the ongoing UN climate summit (COP31) in Turkey is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (£30bn) baseline that it says developed countries committed to providing by 2025. The interpretation of that commitment remains contested The proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations at the summit, although African negotiators have continued to push for it The funding is intended to help vulnerable countries prepare for and withstand climate change-induced extreme weather, such as droughts, floods and wildfires But the European Union, one of the largest providers of climate finance, says the priority should be ensuring existing commitments reach vulnerable countries rather than setting new funding targets "We haven't come to the table with additional monies or additional capital. It's about what we have committed already and ensuring it's deployed," Darragh O'Brien, who leads the EU delegation at COP31 on behalf of the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, told a press conference He acknowledged that developing countries faced difficulties accessing available funding, saying the process needed to be improved Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commission's climate commissioner, also argued that the summit should focus on delivering existing pledges rather than making new ones "If you are a vulnerable nation in the Pacific or one of the LDCs (Least Developed Countries) and the money is in the bank but does not land on the ground then it is effectively meaningless," he said 'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El Niño with floods predicted A really simple guide to climate change Hoekstra said the EU had provided $30bn of the $100bn in climate finance committed by developed countries in recent years, adding that other wealthy nations should contribute more The scale of the need is substantial. According to the UN's Adaptation Gap Report published last year, sub-Saharan Africa requires about $51bn annually in adaptation finance, while the Middle East and North Africa needs $112bn Globally, developing countries will need about $300bn annually by 2035, according to the UN's latest report. Yet they received only about 10% of that amount from developed countries in 2024 Climate-related loss and damage in Africa is projected to cost $440bn between 2020 and 2030, according to Nairobi-based think tank Power Shift Africa Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation But why have so many African countries failed to prepare plans that could help them identify their needs and build resilience? "If you look closely, the countries that are yet to submit their NAPs are already dealing with multiple crises, including debt distress, economic pressures and other issues," said David Abudho, climate justice lead at the aid agency, Oxfam "Their governments' ability to invest in climate adaptation is limited." Sheila Apiny, regional climate justice adviser at ActionAid, said the lack of plans reflected a wider shortage of financial and technical support "The absence of NAPs in so many countries is, in itself, evidence of an adaptation finance and capacity gap," she argued She said this created a vicious cycle - countries lack support to prepare their plans, while not having the plans makes it harder to secure funding for climate resilience "When countries lack adequate adaptation planning and, more importantly, the resources to implement those plans, governments are forced into a cycle of responding to disasters instead of preventing or reducing their impacts," said Amos Wemanya, senior climate adviser at Power Shift Africa "Instead of investing in early warning systems, climate-resilient agriculture, water security and flood protection, scarce public resources are repeatedly diverted towards emergency relief and reconstruction. This costs more over time and leaves communities increasingly vulnerable." African negotiators acknowledge that adaptation plans help countries prioritise investments and attract funding, but argue that their absence should not be used to deny them financial support "Of course, having a comprehensive NAP helps countries prioritise investments and prepare proposals for climate finance," said Mahlet Eyassu Melkie, a senior strategic adviser to Ethiopia's COP32 presidency "But Africa's adaptation financing needs are based on scientific assessments, climate vulnerability, national priorities and regional estimates – not simply on whether every country has submitted a particular planning document." The UN Development Programme, which has helped more than 45 countries prepare their plans, said NAPs can help governments mobilise international support and coordinate climate action Fred Njehu, a Pan-African political strategist at Greenpeace Africa, said their absence could nevertheless create significant obstacles "It is fair to acknowledge that missing adaptation plans act as a major functional barrier that severely bottlenecks the speed, volume and quality of international funding a country can access," he said But having a plan does not guarantee the money needed to implement it "Even countries that have completed their NAPs have not received money anywhere near what they require for implementation of their adaptation plans," Apiny said Kenya offers an example of how adaptation measures can help communities cope with climate pressures In the country's arid and semi-arid south-east, concrete sand dams slow the flow of seasonal rivers, allowing sand to accumulate and store water underground. Communities can access it during dry periods using hand pumps or by scooping it out UK charity Sand Dams Worldwide and its local partner, the Africa Sand Dam Foundation, said they had built about 1,300 such dams, improving access to water as droughts become more frequent and intense But many vulnerable communities elsewhere on the continent are still waiting for similar interventions Back in drought-hit Karamoja, Lobur wonders how different things might have been if farmers had access to small-scale irrigation schemes "We do have some underground water sources in some places. If there were proper plans and programmes, we could have tapped them to grow food, but we are having to live in hunger instead," Lobur said "My grandmother keeps reminding us how she lost eight children during a famine-like situation in 1982, and we all fear we might perish like that too." selected_news.quality_narration: Uganda’nın kuzey Karamoja bölgesinde 44 yaşındaki çiftçi Elijah Lobur ve ailesi, şiddetli kuraklık nedeniyle günde sadece bir öğün yiyebiliyor. Bölgede %90’ın üzerindeki ekinler kurarken, Sand Dams Worldwide ve Africa Sand Dam Foundation gibi kuruluşlar 1.300 sand dam inşa ederek su erişimini artırmayı hedefliyor. Lobur, yer altı su kaynakları ve küçük ölçekli sulama planları olsaydı açlıkla mücadele edebileceklerini belirtiyor.

selected_news.title: India Türkiyeyi UN'da Üye Devletleri Dışlamaktan Kınadı
selected_news.summary: 'Blatant and intentional': India slams Turkey over exclusion from UNGA draft consultations The Times of India
selected_news.source_headline: 'Blatant and intentional': India slams Turkey over exclusion from UNGA draft consultations
selected_news.article_text: India slammed Turkey at the United Nations for its "blatant and intentional" decision to exclude New Delhi and other member states from consultations on a resolution on cooperation between the UN and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC).India voted against the draft resolution, which was adopted by the UN General Assembly with 112 votes in favour, six against and 39 abstentions. Armenia, Cyprus, Greece, Israel and the US also voted against it. Iraq introduced the resolution, while Turkey served as its facilitator.India's deputy permanent representative to the UN Yojna Patel said the OIC's Permanent Observer Mission chose to exclude the Indian delegation and a number of other countries while circulating successive drafts of the resolution.While delivering India's explanation of vote, Patel also called for an investigation into the working methods adopted by the resolution's facilitator."My delegation has voted against this resolution not only because of its substantive aspects, but also for an even more concerning matter regarding the working methods adopted by the facilitator who convened negotiations on the same," Patel said. "This is not only shocking but also sets a bad precedent of delegations excluding specific member states to enable their agendas," she added. Patel also said that despite some delegations registering their objections in subsequent rounds, the "facilitators still chose to not include select countries". Other basic procedures, such as acknowledging inputs, were also "blatantly disregarded", indicating that the exclusion was by design rather than by mistake.She said it was "unfortunate that there are member states who publicly profess commitment to multilateralism and completely turn a blind eye to its core guiding principles".Underlining that the UN was founded on the principles of sovereign equality, inclusivity and multilateral cooperation, Patel said differences of position among member states were inherent to multilateral diplomacy and "cannot, in themselves, justify blatant and intentional exclusion from the consultations on matters before the General Assembly"."My delegation strongly objects to such working methods that try to hoodwink excluded delegations into believing that this was just a technical update, which it was not," she said.In a thinly veiled reference to Pakistan, India also voiced regret that the OIC had "once again allowed itself to be systematically misused by one member state to weaponise OIC resolutions and declarations against India through false and baseless allegations". Pakistan is a founding and prominent member of the 57-member OIC.Greece and Cyprus also raised "serious concerns" regarding the conduct of negotiations under Turkiye's facilitation."Throughout the process, the European Union submitted comments and amendments in good faith, which were neither meaningfully addressed nor accompanied by substantial explanations for their rejection. Furthermore, revised drafts were circulated without adequate consultation," Greece's delegate said. Rohitashwa Ranjan is a digital journalist with The Times of India, where he decodes Indian politics as a carefully staged production with scripts, subtext and everything behind. His stories track elections, party dynamics and the things that often are buried beneath the headlines. When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside

selected_news.shorts_hook: India, Türkiye'nin dışlamasını kınadı: Uluslararası neden?
selected_news.quality_hook: India, Türkiye'nin dışlamasını kınadı: Uluslararası neden?
selected_news.quality_narration: Hindistan, Birleşmiş Milletler'de Türkiye'nin OIC iş birliği taslağını yürütürken bazı ülkeleri dışlamasını "açık ve kasıtlı" olarak eleştirdi. Hindistan'ın BM Daimi Temsilcisi Yojna Patel, bu dışlamanın çoklu taraflılık ilkesine aykırı olduğunu ve bir soruşturma talep ettiğini belirtti. Türkiye, taslağın kolaylaştırıcısı konumunda olsa da, Yunanistan ve Kıbrıs gibi ülkeler de benzer endişelerini dile getirdi.
